title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC; 123680) on chromosome 2q33.3.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC).
checks.evidence_quote: To our knowledge, these findings are the first evidence of an involvement of CRYGC and support the role of CRYGD in human cataract formation.
checks.explanation: The abstract links CRYGC to Coppock-like cataract in one family. It does not mention heterozygosity, multiple cataract types or microcornea.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33.3.
checks.evidence_quote: We recently mapped the aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin locus (CRYG) on chromosome 2q33-35
checks.explanation: The paper places the CRYG cluster at 2q33-35. The draft's 2q33.3 is a standard restatement of the gene's location.

paragraphs.text: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital lens opacity. Families with CRYGC mutations have shown different types of cataract: Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus, highly variable zonular pulverulent cataract, and nuclear congenital cataract. In some families the nuclear cataract was accompanied by microcornea, nystagmus, and amblyopia.

checks.explanation: The abstract supports a Coppock-like cataract family with a CRYGC mutation. It does not say the cataract involves the embryonic lens nucleus.

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family with autosomal dominant congenital cataract of the pulverulent type. Of 138 individuals, 48 were known to be affected. Of the 53 individuals examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: 19 had unilateral cataract (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 had bilateral cataract. The cataract appeared seemingly at random as unilateral or bilateral. Including historic data, there were 48 affected members: 28 with unilateral cataract, 17 with bilateral cataract, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined. In patients with unilateral cataract, detailed slit-lamp examination of the clinically unaffected eye showed no lens opacity. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, through bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgical removal.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation family from northern China in which 6 members had nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, with a central nuclear opacity affecting the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had congenitally small eyeballs and corneas with a diameter of approximately 9 to 10 mm. Every affected individual had the same poor visual acuity of hand movement in front of the eye, and all had nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family with isolated bilateral autosomal dominant nuclear cataracts and microcornea. All affected individuals had bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea with a diameter of approximately 9 mm. The opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, with normal intraocular pressure and no systemic abnormalities. The proband (II:7), a man, was diagnosed with bilateral nuclear cataract and microcornea at age 8 years. He underwent iridectomy on both eyes at age 8, and phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation in the left eye at age 38. Individual I:2 was examined at age 68 years. Individual II:2 was diagnosed at age 13 years. Individual III:3 had cataract extraction at age 6 years. Individuals III:6 and IV:1 were first diagnosed at ages 6 months and 1 year, respectively.

paragraphs.text: Lubsen et al. (1987) found that polymorphic TaqI sites in the gamma-crystallin gene cluster could define 8 possible haplotypes. Only 3 of these (Q, R, and S) were found in the Dutch and English population. A fourth haplotype (P) was found in a family with hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus. Haplotype P was present only in family members with cataract, and all family members with cataract had haplotype P. The cataract locus was closely linked to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0. Lubsen et al. (1987) concluded that the primary cause of a human cataract could possibly be a lesion in a crystallin gene.

paragraphs.text: In the original Coppock-like cataract family, Héon et al. (1999) identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. The mutation was not seen in a large control population. They also found that the change in the CRYGE pseudogene previously reported as the Coppock-like cataract mutation was a polymorphism present in 23% of their control population. They noted that, to date, there was no direct evidence that up-regulation of a pseudogene causes cataracts. Héon et al. (1999) concluded that their findings were the first evidence that CRYGC is involved in human cataract formation.

paragraphs.text: Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-D gene cluster in affected members of a family with autosomal dominant nuclear congenital cataract. They identified a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in the CRYGC gene, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the cataract. Healthy family members and 170 unrelated controls had a normal sequence. Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) concluded that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation and should no longer be considered a SNP, as it was listed in the NCBI database.
